Humans spent one third of their whole lives in this room, lying down with their eyes closed, completely unconscious, on purpose, every single night.
It's called a bedroom, and today I'm going to find out how humans slept before any of this existed.
The door is stuck, so I'll use the window. The ceiling held up, but there's two meters of dirt on the carpet. Scanning?
Posters on the walls, clothes on the floor, a cup with something green growing inside. This human was not tidy.
eight human artifacts in one small room, all of them for the same activity, doing nothing for eight hours. Let's dig!

First artifact a rectangle full of metal springs wrapped in foam and fabric Humans lay on top of it and stayed there all night My scan says it's one of the most expensive objects in the house and it's for sleeping
So, what did humans sleep on before springs? Let's go back, way back.

200,000 years ago, in a cave in South Africa, humans pulled up grass and laid it on the floor to sleep on. Under the grass, they spread ash from the fire. Scientists think it kept crawling insects away from their bodies. The first mattress came with built-in bug spray.

Then for thousands of years, not much changed. In medieval Europe, most people slept on sacks stuffed with straw, and the straw had guests, fleas, lice, bedbugs. Everyone just accepted them as part of the bed. Rich people changed the straw more often. Most people changed it about once a year.
Humans invented springs. The bugs still haven't left.
Second artifact a soft bag for the head humans hugged it folded it flipped it over to find the cold side

The first pillows we know of come from Mesopotamia around 9,000 years ago. They were made of stone. In ancient Egypt, rich people rested their heads on carved wooden headrests and they took them into their tombs. In China, people slept on porcelain pillows, hard and cool, with paintings on the sides.
Humans used to sleep on rocks and they liked it.

And no, people in the Middle Ages didn't sleep sitting up. The paintings show them propped up on pillows, but that's mostly just how artists drew beds. Some doctors told sick people to keep their heads up. Everyone else slept lying down, like you.
Third artifact a heavy blanket big enough for two humans my scan found hairs from four different people on it including a dog

For most of history, sleeping alone was rare. Whole families shared one bed to stay warm. When humans traveled, the inn could put you in a bed with a total stranger. And there were rules. Lie still, stay quiet, and don't steal the blankets.

In 1776, two American Founding Fathers, John Adams and Benjamin Franklin, had to share a tiny bed at a crowded inn. Adams closed the window because he was afraid of the cold night air. Franklin opened it again and lectured him about his theory of colds, until Adams fell asleep.
A future president and a scientist fighting over a window, I would have closed it too.
Human body manual page one why do humans shut down every night?

While you're awake, your brain works non-stop, and it makes waste. When you fall asleep, a fluid washes through your brain and carries that waste away. In a famous study with mice, the spaces between brain cells opened up by about 60% during sleep, so the cleaning could flow faster.
So every night your brain takes out the trash. Adults need about seven hours to do it properly.
I recharge in 40 minutes. Just saying.
Fourth artifact, a lamp. You press a button and the night is gone.

Before electricity, light was expensive. Poor families burned candles made of animal fat that smoked and smelled terrible. Or a rush light, a dried plant dipped in grease that burned for about 20 minutes.

So when the sun went down, the night was really really dark, and historian Roger Eckertsch found hundreds of old diaries and letters that describe something strange. People went to bed a few hours after dark, then woke up around midnight for an hour or so. They prayed, talked, visited the neighbors, and then went back to bed. They called it first sleep and second sleep.
Then cheap artificial light arrived, people started staying up later, and the two sleeps slowly turned into one.
Human body manual page 2 what happens inside the shutdown human?

Sleep comes in cycles of about 90 minutes, and in 1953, two scientists in Chicago noticed something weird every so often sleeping people's eyes start moving fast under their eyelids. They called it REM, rapid eye movement, wake someone up during it, and they'll usually tell you a dream.
So every night humans lie completely still while their eyes watch a movie that doesn't exist

Back to the present. The wardrobe collapsed, so I'm digging around it. One more drawer, and the drawer is full of the same soft clothes. 27 pieces, and all of them with little moons on them. This human had a favorite.
Fifth artifact. Soft clothes with little moons printed on them. Humans wear them only to sleep.

The word pajamas comes from Persian, pie, leg, and jama, clothing, leg clothes. The British picked them up in India in the 1800s and took them home as sleepwear. Before that, most Europeans slept in a long night shirt.
Sixth artifact, a small table next to the bed. Today it holds a phone, a glass of water, and a book nobody finishes.

But before indoor toilets, its main job was hiding the chamber pot, a little cabinet with a door so you didn't have to see it. In fancy French houses, that kind of cabinet was called a commode. And that's why today, a toilet can be called a commode.
Your nightstand used to be a toilet closet. I'm not touching it.
7th artifact. Two small foam cylinders. Humans pushed them into their ears to block out other humans.

The oldest earplugs in any story are made of beeswax. In Homer's Odyssey, Odysseus plugs his sailor's ears so they won't hear the deadly song of the sirens. Then in 1907, a German pharmacist named Max Negwer read that story and started selling wax earplugs. His company still makes them today.
My scan says this pair was used a lot. Somebody in this house snored.
8th Artifact, a phone still plugged in next to the pillow. Its last setting, an alarm at 6.30, snoozed 8 times.
The same object was the alarm, the clock, the lamp, the radio, and the bedtime story. Humans took the whole world into bed with them and then wondered why they couldn't sleep.

Operators who watched my last expedition already know this one. Before alarm clocks, workers paid a knocker upper to tap on their windows or shoot dried peas at them. And in 1956, humans invented the snooze button.
Human body manual page 3 what happens if a human doesn't sleep at all?

In 1964, a 17-year-old named Randy Gardner stayed awake for 11 days straight. For a school science project, by day 3, he was moody and clumsy. By day 5, he was seeing things that weren't there. He slept 14 hours afterwards and recovered. Guinness later stopped tracking the record, because it's too dangerous.
Dolphins do it smarter. They sleep with half of their brain at a time and keep one eye open.

Let me check my inventory. Eight artifacts. Grass beds, stone pillows, strangers sharing blankets. Two sleeps a night, pajamas from Persia, a toilet cabinet, wax from the odyssey, and peas against the window.
So here's my conclusion about humans. For 200,000 years, you worked on the perfect bed, grass, straw, springs, foam, and then you put a glowing rectangle next to your pillow that keeps you awake.

But there's one more artifact. It was hidden under the bed. A glass bottle full of liquid with a blob of wax inside that slowly floats up. And slowly sinks down over and over. It doesn't light the room, it doesn't tell the time, and it doesn't make a sound.
